claim: Repeated exposure to drugs of abuse results in an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the mesolimbic dopamine system.
source: Repeated exposure to drugs of abuse results in an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the mesolimbic dopamine system, a molecular adaptation thought to be critically involved in the development of drug dependence.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Epac2 is a major cAMP effector abundantly expressed in the brain.
source: Exchange protein directly activated by cAMP (Epac2) is a major cAMP effector abundantly expressed in the brain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Conditional knockout of Epac2 from midbrain dopamine neurons decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules.
source: Conditional knockout of Epac2 from midbrain dopamine neurons (Epac2-cKO) and the selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules and across a broad range of cocaine doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2A-G showing reduced cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.

claim: The selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules.
source: Conditional knockout of Epac2 from midbrain dopamine neurons (Epac2-cKO) and the selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules and across a broad range of cocaine doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1B-H showing dose-dependent reduction in cocaine self-administration with ESI-05 treatment.

claim: Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
source: In addition, Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release, whereas Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4 showing decreased dopamine release in Epac2-cKO mice.

claim: Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
source: In addition, Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release, whereas Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5 showing increased dopamine release with S-220 (Epac2 agonist) treatment.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons via DCZ-induced activation of Gs-DREADD increased dopamine release and reversed the impairment of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.
source: This mechanism is central to the behavioral effects of Epac2 disruption, as chemogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons via deschloroclozapine (DCZ)-induced activation of Gs-DREADD increased dopamine release and reversed the impairment of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6 showing restoration of cocaine self-administration with rM3D(Gs) activation.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons with Gi-DREADD reduced dopamine release and cocaine self-administration in wild-type mice.
source: Conversely, chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons with Gi-DREADD reduced dopamine release and cocaine self-administration in wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7 showing reduced cocaine self-administration with hM4D(Gi) activation.

claim: The rewarding effects of cocaine are primarily mediated by enhanced dopaminergic transmission in the mesolimbic dopamine system.
source: The rewarding effects of cocaine are primarily mediated by enhanced dopaminergic transmission in the mesolimbic dopamine system (Anderson and Pierce, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson and Pierce, 2005.

claim: Repeated cocaine exposure induces an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the VTA and NAc.
source: Repeated cocaine exposure induces an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) (Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Nestler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Nestler, 2016.

claim: Repeated cocaine exposure decreases Gαi/o expression in the VTA, which results in elevated cAMP levels.
source: In the VTA, repeated cocaine exposure has been shown to decrease Gαi/o expression (Nestler et al., 1990; Striplin and Kalivas, 1992), which results in elevated cAMP levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nestler et al., 1990; Striplin and Kalivas, 1992.

claim: PKA and Epac are two major intracellular cAMP effectors.
source: Protein kinase A (PKA) and exchange protein directly activated by cAMP (Epac) are two major intracellular cAMP effectors (de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012) and have numerous downstream signaling targets, thereby transducing changes in cAMP levels to cellular adaptations that can promote behavioral changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Epac2 is predominately expressed in the brain, whereas Epac1 expression in the brain is very low.
source: Epac2 is predominately expressed in the brain, whereas Epac1 expression in the brain is very low (de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claim: Epac2, but not Epac1, regulates adaptations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity in VTA dopamine neurons induced by non-contingent cocaine exposure.
source: By making whole-cell recordings in ex vivo slices prepared from Epac1 and Epac2 global knockout mice (Yang et al., 2012), we have shown that Epac2, but not Epac1, regulates adaptations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity in VTA dopamine neurons induced by non-contingent cocaine exposure (Liu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Liu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2017) and Yang et al., 2012.

claim: Epac activators enhance presynaptic glutamate release by increasing the association between the active zone proteins Rab3A, RIM and Munc13, thereby facilitating vesicle docking and exocytosis.
source: Epac activators enhance presynaptic glutamate release by increasing the association between the active zone proteins Rab3A, RIM and Munc13, thereby facilitating vesicle docking and exocytosis (Ozaki et al., 2000; Ferrero et al., 2013; Fernandes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ozaki et al., 2000; Ferrero et al., 2013; Fernandes et al., 2015.

claim: Axonal dopamine release in the striatum is mediated by vesicular exocytosis and requires active zone-like site machinery.
source: Axonal dopamine release in the striatum is mediated by vesicular exocytosis and requires active zone-like site machinery (Liu and Kaeser, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu and Kaeser, 2019.

claim: Dopamine neuron-specific knockout of RIM abolished action potential-triggered dopamine release in the striatum.
source: Dopamine neuron-specific knockout of RIM abolished action potential-triggered dopamine release in the striatum (Liu et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018a.

claim: The average number of sessions to reach stable acquisition of cocaine self-administration was 5.4±0.3 sessions.
source: The average number of sessions to reach stable acquisition was 5.4±0.3 sessions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A showing training sessions.

claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes during cocaine self-administration.
source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing dose-dependent reduction in active nose pokes with ESI-05 treatment.

claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced cocaine infusions during self-administration.
source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C showing dose-dependent reduction in cocaine infusions with ESI-05 treatment.

claim: ESI-05 had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes during cocaine self-administration.
source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D showing no significant effect on inactive nose pokes.

claim: No significant sex differences were observed for cocaine self-administration measures.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Slosky et al., 2021), no significant sex differences were observed for any measure, thus the data were pooled across sexes in subsequent studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data and a citation to Slosky et al., 2021.

claim: ESI-05 pretreatments produced a significant downward shift in the dose-response curve for cocaine infusions.
source: ESI-05 pretreatments produced a significant downward shift in the dose-response curve for cocaine infusions (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA: ESI-05 treatment, F2,22 = 45.5, p<0.001; cocaine dose, F6,132 = 51.0, p<0.001; ESI-05 treatment × cocaine dose interaction, F12,132 = 6.5, p<0.001; 3.3 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, red *; 10 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, violet *; 3.3 vs. 10 mg/kg ESI-05 black #) and decreased total cocaine intake (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA: ESI-05 treatment, F2,22 = 66.5, p<0.001; cocaine dose, F6,132 = 498.1, p<0.001; ESI-05 × cocaine dose interaction, F12,132 = 6.7, p<0.001; 3.3 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, red *; 10 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05 violet *; 3.3 vs. 10 mg/kg ESI-05 black #) on the dose-response curve (n=8–9, 5 male and 4 female).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1E-F.

claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions under a PR reinforcement schedule.
source: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions (one-way ANOVA: F2,28 = 16.1, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) and breakpoint (Brown-Forsythe equal variance: p<0.05; Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA on ranks: ESI-05, H=17.5, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) under a PR reinforcement schedule.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1G-H.

claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
source: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions (one-way ANOVA: F2,28 = 16.1, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) and breakpoint (Brown-Forsythe equal variance: p<0.05; Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA on ranks: ESI-05, H=17.5, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) under a PR reinforcement schedule.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice and WT controls were grossly normal in terms of survival, physical appearance, body weight, and baseline locomotor activity.
source: Epac2-cKO mice (Slc6a3IREScre/+/Epac2loxP/loxP) and WT controls (Slc6a3IREScre/+/Epac2wt/wt or Slc6a3+/+/Epac2loxP/loxP) were grossly normal in terms of survival, physical appearance, body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and baseline locomotor activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice.
source: We found that Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Epac2 was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice.
source: We found that Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Epac1 was rarely expressed in neurons of WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
source: Epac1 was rarely expressed in neurons of WT and Epac2-cKO mice, consistent with low expression of Epac1 in the brain (Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data and a citation to Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claim: There were no significant differences in the frequency of action potential firing or membrane capacitance in VTA dopamine neurons between WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
source: We also compared the electrophysiological properties of VTA dopamine neurons from WT and Epac2-cKO mice and found no significance differences in the frequency of action potential firing or membrane capacitance (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no significant difference between the percentage of WT and Epac2-cKO mice that acquired stable cocaine self-administration after 10 sessions.
source: There was no significant difference between the percentage of mice in each genotype that acquired stable cocaine self-administration after 10 sessions, with 90.9% (10 of 11) of WT and 84.6% (11 of 13) of Epac2-cKO mice with patent catheters meeting the criteria for stable self-administration (χ2=0.024, p=0.877).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acquisition rates.

claim: The average number of training sessions to reach criteria for stable self-administration was not significantly different between WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
source: Of the mice that acquired stable self-administration, the average number of training sessions to reach criteria was not significantly different between genotypes (WT, 5.4±0.5 sessions; Epac2-cKO, 6.8±0.7 sessions; t19=1.6, p=0.130).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of training sessions.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes during cocaine self-administration training.
source: However, Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes (Figure 2A) and cocaine infusions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in cocaine infusions during self-administration training.
source: However, Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes (Figure 2A) and cocaine infusions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Inactive nose pokes were not significantly different between WT and Epac2-cKO mice during cocaine self-administration.
source: Inactive nose pokes were not significantly different between genotypes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice exhibited a downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve.
source: Epac2-cKO mice displayed a significant downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve compared with WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice exhibited lower cocaine intake than WT mice across multiple cocaine doses.
source: Epac2-cKO mice also exhibited lower cocaine intake than WT mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions under a PR reinforcement schedule.
source: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions (Figure 2F) and had a significantly reduced breakpoint (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice had a significantly reduced breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
source: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions (Figure 2F) and had a significantly reduced breakpoint (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: ESI-05 had no significant effect on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake under an FR1 reinforcement schedule.
source: ESI-05 had no significant effect on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: ESI-05 did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
source: Again, ESI-05 did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) under this reinforcement schedule.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Epac2-cKO did not affect the acquisition of sucrose self-administration under an FR1 schedule.
source: Under an FR1 schedule, there was no significant effect of genotype on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake across the 10-day session (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Epac2-cKO did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR schedule.
source: Similarly, Epac2-cKO did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR schedule (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
source: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse and high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
source: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse and high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4D-E.

claim: There were no significant changes in the exponential decay constant τ of evoked dopamine responses from either single pulse or high-frequency burst stimulation across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
source: We found that there were no significant changes in τ from either single pulse or high-frequency burst stimulation across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, C, D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4C and F.

claim: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices.
source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The S-220-induced increase in evoked dopamine release was blocked by Epac2-cKO.
source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The S-220-induced increase in evoked dopamine release was blocked by ESI-05.
source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The PKA inhibitor H89 had no effect on the S-220-induced increase in dopamine release.
source: In contrast, the PKA inhibitor H89 (1 μM) had no effect (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Bath application of 6-Bnz-cAMP increased dopamine release in the NAc shell in slices from WT mice.
source: Bath application of 6-Bnz-cAMP (1 µM) increased dopamine release in the NAc shell in slices from WT mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The 6-Bnz-cAMP-induced increase in dopamine release was blocked by H89.
source: This effect was blocked by H89 but was not altered by Epac-cKO (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The 6-Bnz-cAMP-induced increase in dopamine release was not altered by Epac2-cKO.
source: This effect was blocked by H89 but was not altered by Epac-cKO (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: rM3D(Gs) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
source: rM3D(Gs) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons (85.3 ± 4.2% and 87.1 ± 5.3%, respectively) but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: DCZ significantly increased the frequency of dopamine transients in the NAc shell of Epac2-cKO mice following vehicle pretreatment.
source: Subcutaneous injection of DCZ (100 µg/kg) 20 min after i.p. vehicle pretreatment caused a rapid and robust increase (~30 min) in the frequency of dopamine transients in the NAc shell, which was followed by a more modest and sustained increase lasting for the duration of the fiber photometry recordings (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Pretreatment with the PKA inhibitor H89 blocked the effect of DCZ to increase dopamine transient frequency.
source: Pretreatment with the PKA inhibitor H89 (1 mg/kg, i.p.) blocked the effect of DCZ to increase dopamine transient frequency (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice under an FR1 schedule.
source: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes (Figure 6E) and cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: DCZ increased the number of cocaine infusions in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice under an FR1 schedule.
source: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes (Figure 6E) and cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or cocaine infusions in mCherry-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
source: In contrast, DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes (Figure 6E), or cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in mCherry-expressing Epac2-cKO mice, indicating that the effects of DCZ are mediated by rM3D(Gs) activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E-F.

claim: DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons.
source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: DCZ did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector.
source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: hM4D(Gi) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
source: hM4D(Gi) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons (83.8 ± 4.1% and 84.7 ± 3.4%, respectively) but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: DCZ significantly decreased dopamine transient frequency in the NAc shell of mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) but not mCherry.
source: Subcutaneous injection of DCZ (100 µg/kg) significantly decreased dopamine transient frequency in the NAc shell of mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) but not mCherry (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: DCZ significantly decreased active nose pokes in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice.
source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: DCZ significantly decreased cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice.
source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice.
source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7D-E.

claim: DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons.
source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: DCZ did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry.
source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: Epac2-mediated enhancement of dopamine release may represent a novel and powerful mechanism that contributes to cocaine reinforcement.
source: Epac2-mediated enhancement of dopamine release may therefore represent a novel and powerful mechanism that contributes to cocaine reinforcement.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Epac2 in the mesolimbic dopamine system promotes cocaine reinforcement via enhancement of dopamine release.
source: Here, we report that Epac2 in the mesolimbic dopamine system promotes cocaine reinforcement via enhancement of dopamine release.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling pathway has been extensively studied in the context of drug addiction.
source: The cAMP-PKA-CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) signaling pathway has been extensively studied in the context of drug addiction (Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Nestler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: Few studies have addressed how Epac regulates the cellular and behavioral effects of drugs of abuse.
source: However, few studies have addressed how the 'other' cAMP effector, Epac, regulates the cellular and behavioral effects of drugs of abuse.
evidence: This claim establishes the novelty and rationale for the current study.

claim: Drug self-administration provides a measure of the reinforcing efficacy of drugs of abuse and an animal's motivation to acquire rewarding drugs.
source: Drug self-administration provides a measure of the reinforcing efficacy of drugs of abuse and an animal's motivation to acquire rewarding drugs (O'Connor et al., 2011; Hiranita, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Connor et al., 2011; Hiranita, 2015.

claim: Cocaine and sucrose increase dopamine levels by reducing its uptake and increasing its release, respectively.
source: Cocaine and sucrose increase dopamine levels by reducing its uptake and increasing its release, respectively (Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claim: Similar differential modulation of cocaine vs. sucrose self-administration by pharmacological agents has been reported.
source: However, similar differential modulation of cocaine vs. sucrose self-administration by pharmacological agents has been reported (Levy et al., 2007; Romieu et al., 2008; Mu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levy et al., 2007; Romieu et al., 2008; Mu et al., 2021.

claim: The majority of NAc neurons exhibited different firing patterns in response to food and cocaine rewards.
source: Although there is significant overlap in the neuronal circuits encoding food and drug rewards (Volkow et al., 2012), the majority of NAc neurons exhibited different firing patterns in response to food and cocaine rewards (Carelli, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Volkow et al., 2012 and Carelli, 2002.

claim: Epac agonism facilitates vesicle exocytosis by interacting with the active zone proteins RIM and Munc13.
source: Epac agonism was shown to facilitate vesicle exocytosis by interacting with the active zone proteins RIM and Munc13 (Ozaki et al., 2000; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ozaki et al., 2000; Tengholm and Gylfe, 2017.

claim: RIM is clustered in dopamine axons.
source: RIM is clustered in dopamine axons, and conditional knockout of RIM from midbrain dopamine neurons abolished action potential-triggered dopamine release (Liu and Kaeser, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu and Kaeser, 2019.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic interneurons in the NAc induced dopamine release via activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic interneurons in the NAc induced dopamine release via activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) (Cachope et al., 2012; Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cachope et al., 2012; Threlfell et al., 2012.

claim: GABA tonically depresses axonal dopamine release in the dorsal striatum via GABAA and GABAB receptors.
source: GABA tonically depresses axonal dopamine release in the dorsal striatum via GABAA and GABAB receptors (Roberts et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2020.

claim: Drugs of abuse including cocaine increase dopamine levels in the NAc, which is thought to underlie their reinforcing effects.
source: Drugs of abuse including cocaine increase dopamine levels in the NAc, which is thought to underlie their reinforcing effects (Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Volkow et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Volkow et al., 2006.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons via hM4D(Gi) suppressed heroin self-administration under an FR1 reinforcement schedule.
source: Similarly, chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons via hM4D(Gi) suppressed heroin self-administration under an FR1 reinforcement schedule (Corre et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Corre et al., 2018.

claim: Knockdown of D2 autoreceptors in midbrain dopamine neurons increased dopamine levels due to reduced autoinhibition and caused a general upward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve.
source: Conversely, knockdown of D2 autoreceptors in midbrain dopamine neurons increased dopamine levels due to reduced autoinhibition and caused a general upward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Gq-DREADD-mediated stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons potentiated cue and cocaine-priming induced reinstatement, whereas Gi-DREADD reduced reinstatement.
source: Further, Gq-DREADD-mediated stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons potentiated cue and cocaine-priming induced reinstatement, whereas Gi-DREADD reduced reinstatement (Mahler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mahler et al., 2018.

claim: Epac signals downstream via myriad effectors, including Rap, Ras, Rho, phospholipase C, and mitogen-activated protein kinases.
source: Epac signals downstream via myriad effectors, including Rap, Ras, Rho, phospholipase C, and mitogen-activated protein kinases (Laurent et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurent et al., 2012.

claim: Epac can be activated by both cAMP-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: Epac can be activated by both cAMP-dependent and -independent mechanisms (Shibasaki et al., 2004; Baameur et al., 2016; Robichaux and Cheng, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shibasaki et al., 2004; Baameur et al., 2016; Robichaux and Cheng, 2018.

claim: Repeated cocaine administration induces structural plasticity in the NAc.
source: Repeated cocaine administration induces structural plasticity in the NAc (Cahill et al., 2016; Barrientos et al., 2018; Kalivas, 2018), of which Rap1 GTPase signaling plays a critical role (Cahill et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cahill et al., 2016; Barrientos et al., 2018; Kalivas, 2018.

claim: Rap1 GTPase signaling plays a critical role in cocaine-induced structural plasticity in the NAc.
source: Repeated cocaine administration induces structural plasticity in the NAc (Cahill et al., 2016; Barrientos et al., 2018; Kalivas, 2018), of which Rap1 GTPase signaling plays a critical role (Cahill et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cahill et al., 2016.

claim: Cocaine self-administration and seeking depend on both dopamine-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: Cocaine self-administration and seeking depend on both dopamine-dependent and -independent mechanisms (Schmidt and Pierce, 2010; Mereu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schmidt and Pierce, 2010; Mereu et al., 2020.

claim: Postsynaptically, Epac2 modulates AMPAR trafficking by inducing changes in AMPAR subunit composition.
source: Postsynaptically, Epac2 modulates AMPAR trafficking by inducing changes in AMPAR subunit composition (Woolfrey et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016) and enhances open-channel probability of GluA3-AMPARs (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Woolfrey et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Epac2 enhances open-channel probability of GluA3-AMPARs.
source: Postsynaptically, Epac2 modulates AMPAR trafficking by inducing changes in AMPAR subunit composition (Woolfrey et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016) and enhances open-channel probability of GluA3-AMPARs (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017.

claim: Presynaptically, Epac2 facilitates glutamate release and enables long-term potentiation.
source: Presynaptically, Epac2 facilitates glutamate release and enables long-term potentiation (LTP) (Fernandes et al., 2015; Martín et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2015; Martín et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic deletion of Epac1/2 or Epac2 led to the impairment of LTP in the hippocampus, spatial social interaction, and spatial learning and memory.
source: Genetic deletion of Epac1/2 or Epac2 led to the impairment of LTP in the hippocampus, spatial social interaction, and spatial learning and memory (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2012.

claim: Addictive drugs such as cocaine induce long-term synaptic plasticity in the reward circuitry of the brain.
source: Addictive drugs such as cocaine induce long-term synaptic plasticity in the reward circuitry of the brain (Wolf, 2016; Dong et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zinsmaier et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wolf, 2016; Dong et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zinsmaier et al., 2022.

claim: Epac2 likely acts via multifactorial mechanisms that together promote cocaine-induced neuroadaptations and drug reinforcement.
source: It is likely that Epac2 acts via multifactorial mechanisms that together promote cocaine-induced neuroadaptations and drug reinforcement.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the discussion of multiple mechanisms.

claim: The Instech self-administration system greatly extends the longevity of catheter patency.
source: We examined the effect of the selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 on cocaine self-administration in roughly equal numbers of male and female mice using an Instech self-administration system that greatly extends the longevity of catheter patency (Slosky et al., 2020; Slosky et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Slosky et al., 2020; Slosky et al., 2021.

claim: 18 of 20 mice with patent catheters acquired stable cocaine self-administration.
source: C57BL/6J mice underwent training for cocaine self-administration under a FR1 reinforcement schedule (0.5 mg/kg/infusion) in 3 hr sessions over 10 days, and 18 of 20 mice with patent catheters acquired stable cocaine self-administration (criteria are detailed in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the training phase.

claim: Vehicle-treated mice exhibited a consistently high rate of cocaine infusions with a predominantly regularly spaced pattern over the entire 3 hr session.
source: Vehicle-treated mice exhibited a consistently high rate of cocaine infusions with a predominantly regularly spaced pattern over the entire 3 hr session; ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced the rate of cocaine infusions, which was characterized by unevenly spaced intervals and sporadic intake, particularly at the higher ESI-05 dose (10 mg/kg, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced the rate of cocaine infusions, which was characterized by unevenly spaced intervals and sporadic intake.
source: Vehicle-treated mice exhibited a consistently high rate of cocaine infusions with a predominantly regularly spaced pattern over the entire 3 hr session; ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced the rate of cocaine infusions, which was characterized by unevenly spaced intervals and sporadic intake, particularly at the higher ESI-05 dose (10 mg/kg, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Maximal cocaine infusions occurred at the 0.125 mg/kg/infusion dose in the multiple-dose paradigm.
source: By using an initial 0.5 mg/kg/infusion followed by descending doses in a single session (1.0, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125, and 0.0 mg/kg/infusion; see Materials and methods) (Anderson et al., 2018), we observed classic inverted U-shaped dose-response curves in C57BL/6J mice, with maximal infusions occurring at the 0.125 mg/kg/infusion dose (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: WT mice typically displayed a high rate of responding at predominantly regular intervals during cocaine self-administration.
source: WT mice typically displayed a high rate of responding at predominantly regular intervals, while Epac2-cKO mice displayed a pattern resembling that of ESI-05-treated mice characterized by sporadic intake interspersed by long gaps (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Epac2-cKO mice displayed a pattern of cocaine intake characterized by sporadic intake interspersed by long gaps.
source: WT mice typically displayed a high rate of responding at predominantly regular intervals, while Epac2-cKO mice displayed a pattern resembling that of ESI-05-treated mice characterized by sporadic intake interspersed by long gaps (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both WT and Epac2-cKO mice displayed a predominantly regularly spaced pattern of sucrose intake over the entire 1 hr session.
source: Both WT and Epac2-cKO mice displayed a predominantly regularly spaced pattern of sucrose intake over the entire 1 hr session, although bursts of high rates of sucrose intake could also be found in both genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dopamine reuptake by the dopamine transporter is the primary mechanism responsible for extracellular dopamine clearance in the brain.
source: Dopamine reuptake by the dopamine transporter (DAT) is the primary mechanism responsible for extracellular dopamine clearance in the brain (Gainetdinov et al., 1998; Benoit-Marand et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gainetdinov et al., 1998; Benoit-Marand et al., 2000.

claim: The exponential decay constant τ of evoked dopamine responses provides a reliable measure for monitoring changes in dopamine reuptake.
source: The exponential decay constant τ of evoked dopamine responses provides a reliable measure for monitoring changes in dopamine reuptake (Yorgason et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yorgason et al., 2011.

claim: Sp-8-BnT-cAMPS ('S-220') is an Epac2-selective agonist with specificity for Epac2 over PKA and Epac1.
source: Sp-8-BnT-cAMPS ('S-220') is an Epac2-selective agonist with specificity for Epac2 over PKA and Epac1 (Schwede et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwede et al., 2015.

claim: 6-Bnz-cAMP is a membrane permeable and selective PKA activator and does not activate Epac.
source: 6-Bnz-cAMP is a membrane permeable and selective PKA activator and does not activate Epac (Christensen et al., 2003; Hewer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2003; Hewer et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of Epac2 and PKA pathways each independently increases evoked dopamine release.
source: Thus, activation of Epac2 and PKA pathways each independently increases evoked dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The AAV expression was predominantly limited to the VTA and was seldom observed in the neighboring SNc.
source: The AAV expression was predominantly limited to the VTA and was seldom observed in the neighboring SNc.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: DCZ is a DREADD actuator that shows greater affinity and potency for DREADDs than clozapine N-oxide, is highly brain-penetrant, and is metabolically stable.
source: DCZ is a DREADD actuator that shows greater affinity and potency for DREADDs than clozapine N-oxide, is highly brain-penetrant, and is metabolically stable (Nagai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nagai et al., 2020.

claim: In vivo two-photon imaging of somatosensory cortex neurons that co-expressed Gq-DREADD (hM3Dq) and GCaMP6 revealed that i.p. injection of DCZ led to a rapid increase in GCaMP6 activity in mice that peaked at about 10 min and plateaued for at least 150 min.
source: In vivo two-photon imaging of somatosensory cortex neurons that co-expressed Gq-DREADD (hM3Dq) and GCaMP6 revealed that i.p. injection of DCZ led to a rapid increase in GCaMP6 activity in mice that peaked at about 10 min and plateaued for at least 150 min.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological consideration for the DREADD experiments.

claim: The increase in operant responding on the ascending limb of the dose-response curve could be attributable to an increase in the reinforcing efficacy of cocaine.
source: The increase in operant responding on the ascending limb could be attributable to an increase in the reinforcing efficacy of cocaine (Mello and Negus, 1996; Caine et al., 2002; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to Mello and Negus, 1996; Caine et al., 2002; Roberts et al., 2013.

claim: rM3D(Gs) activation increases dopamine release, which enhances reinforcement and promotes operant responding at low cocaine unit doses.
source: Since rM3D(Gs) activation increases dopamine release, cocaine infusions at low unit doses likely result in greater dopamine levels, which enhances reinforcement and promotes operant responding (Mello and Negus, 1996; Caine et al., 2002; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results supported by citations.

claim: The DCZ-induced increase in the reinforcing efficacy of cocaine may counter the rate-decreasing effects of higher cocaine unit doses.
source: The DCZ-induced increase in the reinforcing efficacy of cocaine may counter the rate-decreasing effects of higher cocaine unit doses (Zimmer et al., 2011), which may explain why rM3D(Gs) activation did not significantly shift the descending limb.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Zimmer et al., 2011.

claim: The impairment of cocaine self-administration caused by Epac2 disruption is largely reversible with restoration of midbrain dopamine release.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that the impairment of cocaine self-administration caused by Epac2 disruption is largely reversible with restoration of midbrain dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the DREADD rescue experiments.

claim: Bidirectional modulation of dopamine release is capable of enhancing or depressing operant responding for cocaine across multiple unit doses and does not result in a simple shift in cocaine potency.
source: Thus, bidirectional modulation of dopamine release is capable of enhancing or depressing operant responding for cocaine across multiple unit doses and does not result in a simple shift in cocaine potency.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the DREADD experiments and supported by citations.

claim: The dorsal striatum is preferentially innervated by dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), while the NAc is preferentially innervated by VTA dopamine neurons.
source: The dorsal striatum is preferentially innervated by dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), while the NAc is preferentially innervated by VTA dopamine neurons (Ogawa and Watabe Uchida, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogawa and Watabe Uchida, 2018.

claim: GRABDA2m sensors are mutant D2 receptors that increase fluorescence intensity with dopamine binding and retain sensitivity to D2 antagonists.
source: GRABDA2m sensors are mutant D2 receptors that increase fluorescence intensity with dopamine binding and retain sensitivity to D2 antagonists (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The fluorescence transients detected by GRABDA2m were abolished by i.p. injection of the D2 antagonist haloperidol, indicating that the transients are due to dopamine binding the sensor.
source: We found that the fluorescence transients were abolished by i.p. injection of the D2 antagonist haloperidol (0.1 mg/kg, i.p.; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the transients are due to dopamine binding the sensor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RIM mediates vesicle tethering and is required for Ca2+-channel recruitment to release sites.
source: RIM mediates vesicle tethering and is required for Ca2+-channel recruitment to release sites (Acuna et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Acuna et al., 2016.

claim: Epac2 may facilitate dopamine exocytosis from midbrain dopamine neurons by interacting with RIM and other active zone proteins and prompting Ca2+-dependent dopamine release.
source: Epac2 may therefore facilitate dopamine exocytosis from midbrain dopamine neurons by interacting with RIM and other active zone proteins and prompting Ca2+-dependent dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Dopamine axonal terminals are the predominant site for the action of S-220.
source: However, the S-220-induced enhancement of dopamine release was abolished by Epac2-cKO from dopamine neurons, suggesting that dopamine axonal terminals are the predominant site for the action of S-220.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that Epac2-cKO blocks S-220 effects.

claim: Cocaine-mediated DAT inhibition in mice with disrupted Epac2 would cause a lesser increase in extracellular dopamine levels and attenuated dopamine-driven behaviors.
source: As disruption of Epac2 leads to reduced synaptically released dopamine, it is likely that cocaine-mediated DAT inhibition in mice with disrupted Epac2 would cause a lesser increase in extracellular dopamine levels and attenuated dopamine-driven behaviors.
evidence: This claim is a logical inference based on the mechanism of cocaine action and the observed reduction in dopamine release.

claim: Epac2 likely regulates behavior via mechanisms that extend beyond the facilitation of presynaptic dopamine release.
source: It is likely that Epac2 regulates behavior via mechanisms that extend beyond the facilitation of presynaptic dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is a speculative statement acknowledging the complexity of Epac2 signaling.
